revealSteps.title: Blood is the delivery service
revealSteps.body: Blood carries oxygen and food to every body cell and carries waste away.

teacherNotes.ask: Two minutes only. Pupils name what blood carries. Select Red cells, then Plasma. Ask: “So what keeps this delivery moving?”
teacherNotes.listen: Oxygen and food delivered; waste (carbon dioxide) taken away. Red cells carry most of the oxygen; plasma is the liquid that carries food and waste.
teacherNotes.reason: Blood transports materials, but it cannot move itself. That sets up the need for a pump.
teacherNotes.misconception: Blood makes oxygen; or blood is only red cells.
teacherNotes.revisit: Select each component once. White cells and platelets: one sentence each. Do not reteach the Blood lesson.
talkingPoints: Open with the question “What does blood carry?” and take three quick answers before you select anything.
Red cells: they carry most of the oxygen. Select them to show the oxygen they carry.
Plasma: the liquid part. It carries dissolved food and waste such as carbon dioxide.
Bridge to the heart: “Blood carries the supplies. What keeps it moving?” Leave it unanswered for now.

revealSteps.label: THE PROBLEM
revealSteps.title: Blood cannot move by itself
revealSteps.body: The blood is full of useful supplies, but nothing is pushing it.
revealSteps.teacherPrompt: Blood carries the supplies. What could keep it moving?

revealSteps.label: THE HEART IS A MUSCLE
revealSteps.title: Muscle squeezes → blood is pushed
revealSteps.body: When the heart muscle contracts (squeezes), it pushes blood out into the blood vessels. Then it relaxes and fills again. One squeeze + relax = one heartbeat.
revealSteps.teacherPrompt: What do you notice each time the muscle squeezes?

revealSteps.label: NO SQUEEZE, NO PUSH
revealSteps.title: Pump paused: the blood slows and stops
revealSteps.body: Without the heart’s squeeze there is no push, so the blood stops moving. The heart must keep pumping all the time.
revealSteps.teacherPrompt: What does this tell us about the heart’s job?

presentation.fallbackNotice: Moving simulations need Schoolynq player 2.9.4-heart4. Older v2.x players show the labelled diagram, the reveal steps and the questions.

teacherNotes.ask: Start with the model still. Ask what could move the blood. Start the heartbeat, then pause the pump and restart it. Use “One squeeze” to show a single beat.
teacherNotes.listen: The heart muscle contracts (squeezes) and pushes blood. Without the squeeze, the blood stops.
teacherNotes.reason: The heart is a muscular pump. Contraction supplies the force that moves blood through vessels.
teacherNotes.misconception: Blood moves by itself, or oxygen pushes the blood.
teacherNotes.revisit: Pupils clench and relax a fist to feel a squeeze. Press “One squeeze” and ask which part supplied the push.
talkingPoints: Start with the pump paused: nothing moves. Ask what could move the blood.
Start the heartbeat. Each squeeze pushes blood out; each relax lets the heart refill.
Pause the pump: the blood slows and stops. The heart has to keep working all the time.
Body link: pupils clench and relax a fist about once a second for ten seconds.

question.prompt: What gives blood the push to leave the heart?

options.text: The blood moves by itself.
options.feedback: Blood cannot move by itself. The heart muscle supplies the push.

options.text: Oxygen pushes the blood.
options.feedback: Oxygen is cargo carried by blood. It is not a pump.

options.text: The heart muscle contracts (squeezes).
options.feedback: Yes. When the heart muscle contracts, it pushes blood into the blood vessels.

options.text: The ribs squeeze the blood.
options.feedback: The ribs protect the heart and lungs. The heart muscle does the squeezing.

question.explanation: The heart is a muscular pump. When its muscle contracts, it pushes blood into the blood vessels.

correct.headline: Correct. Now explain why.
correct.message: The heart is a muscular pump. When its muscle contracts, it pushes blood into the blood vessels.

incorrect.headline: Let’s fix the idea.
incorrect.message: The heart is a muscular pump. When its muscle contracts, it pushes blood into the blood vessels.

teacherNotes.ask: Ask for the answer AND the evidence from the pump model.
teacherNotes.listen: “The muscle squeezes”, linked to what they saw when the pump was paused.
teacherNotes.reason: Contraction of heart muscle is the cause; blood movement is the effect.
teacherNotes.misconception: Oxygen or the blood itself provides the push.
teacherNotes.revisit: Replay the pump: pause it and ask what stopped.
talkingPoints: Push for a cause-and-effect sentence: “The heart muscle contracts, so blood is pushed into the vessels.”
Option B (oxygen pushes) mixes up cargo and force. Name that mix-up out loud.

revealSteps.label: MEET THE HEART
revealSteps.title: Two sides, four chambers
revealSteps.body: Front view: the person’s RIGHT side is on YOUR left. Each side has an upper chamber (atrium) that collects blood and a lower chamber (ventricle) that pumps it out.
revealSteps.teacherPrompt: Point to the person’s right ventricle. Why is it on our left?

revealSteps.label: THE RIGHT SIDE
revealSteps.title: The right side pumps blood to the lungs
revealSteps.body: Blood from the body collects in the right atrium and drops into the right ventricle. The right ventricle pumps it to the lungs, where oxygen moves into the blood.
revealSteps.teacherPrompt: Watch the lungs. What changes about the blood there?

revealSteps.label: THE LEFT SIDE
revealSteps.title: The left side pumps blood to the body
revealSteps.body: Oxygen-rich blood from the lungs collects in the left atrium and drops into the left ventricle. The left ventricle pumps it out to every part of the body.
revealSteps.teacherPrompt: What does the blood deliver to the body cells?

revealSteps.label: BOTH AT ONCE
revealSteps.title: Both sides squeeze at the same time
revealSteps.body: Each heartbeat: both atria squeeze first (small), then both ventricles squeeze together (big). A wall of muscle (highlighted) keeps the two sides apart, so the two kinds of blood do not mix.
revealSteps.teacherPrompt: Why is it useful that the two kinds of blood do not mix?

revealSteps.label: FOLLOW ONE CELL
revealSteps.title: Twice through the heart on every trip
revealSteps.body: Follow the highlighted cell: body → right side → lungs → left side → body. It passes through the heart twice on every trip around the body.
revealSteps.teacherPrompt: How many times does the cell pass through the heart on one trip?

presentation.fallbackNotice: Moving simulations need Schoolynq player 2.9.4-heart4. Older v2.x players show the labelled diagram, the reveal steps and the questions.

teacherNotes.ask: Step through the five reveals. Let the simulation run; use Slow motion when you want pupils to track colour changes. Select a chamber, a valve or the wall for a one-line explanation. Chamber names are supporting vocabulary: atrium = upper, collects; ventricle = lower, pumps.
teacherNotes.listen: Right side → lungs; left side → body; atrium collects, ventricle pumps; both sides squeeze together; the wall stops mixing; two heart visits per trip.
teacherNotes.reason: Two pumps in one organ, each sending blood to a different destination, beating together. The ventricles do the big push.
teacherNotes.misconception: Viewer’s right = person’s right; the sides take turns; blood mixes inside the heart; the atria do the main pumping.
teacherNotes.revisit: Hold up your own right hand facing the class. Go back to step 1 and point to each chamber in the order blood visits it.
talkingPoints: Orientation first: face the class, raise your right hand and show why it appears on their left.
Four chambers: atria (upper) collect blood, ventricles (lower) pump it out. Names support, they are not assessed.
Steps 2 and 3: trace each loop with your finger on the screen as the cells move.
Step 4: both atria squeeze, then both ventricles squeeze together. The wall (septum) stops the blood mixing.

question.prompt: Which sentence about the two sides of the heart is correct?

options.text: The right side pumps blood to the lungs. The left side pumps blood to the body.
options.feedback: Yes. Each side pumps to a different place: right side → lungs, left side → body.

options.text: Both sides pump blood only to the lungs.
options.feedback: Only the right side pumps to the lungs. The left side pumps to the body.

options.text: Blood flows through the middle wall, so the two kinds of blood mix.
options.feedback: A wall of muscle keeps the two sides apart. Oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor blood do not normally mix.

options.text: The sides take turns: first the right side squeezes, then the left side.
options.feedback: Both sides squeeze at the same time. The slow model follows one cell, so it can look like turns.

question.explanation: The right side pumps blood to the lungs; the left side pumps blood to the body. Both sides squeeze together and the wall keeps their blood apart.

correct.headline: Correct. Now explain why.
correct.message: The right side pumps blood to the lungs; the left side pumps blood to the body. Both sides squeeze together and the wall keeps their blood apart.

incorrect.headline: Let’s fix the idea.
incorrect.message: The right side pumps blood to the lungs; the left side pumps blood to the body. Both sides squeeze together and the wall keeps their blood apart.

teacherNotes.ask: Ask pairs to rule out two wrong answers with a reason before choosing.
teacherNotes.listen: Right → lungs, left → body; “they squeeze together”; “the wall stops mixing”.
teacherNotes.reason: Different destinations for each side; simultaneous beat; separation.
teacherNotes.misconception: Option D (taking turns) is a common result of watching a single-cell animation.
teacherNotes.revisit: Return to step 4 (Both at once) and watch both sides squeeze.
talkingPoints: Ask the spotlight student to rule out one wrong option and say why.
Option D (the sides take turns) comes from watching the slow single-cell model. Correct it explicitly.

revealSteps.label: START AT THE BODY
revealSteps.title: This blood has delivered its oxygen
revealSteps.body: The cell has just passed body cells. It is oxygen-poor (it still has a little oxygen) and it carries waste carbon dioxide.
revealSteps.teacherPrompt: Where will it go first?

revealSteps.label: FIRST HEART VISIT
revealSteps.title: Back to the heart: the right side
revealSteps.body: The blood returns along a vein into the right atrium (upper chamber), then drops through a valve into the right ventricle.

revealSteps.label: PUMPED TO THE LUNGS
revealSteps.title: The right ventricle pushes it to the lungs
revealSteps.body: Watch the squeeze. In the lungs, oxygen moves into the blood and carbon dioxide moves out to be breathed out.

revealSteps.label: PAUSE · PREDICT
revealSteps.title: The blood has picked up oxygen. Why does it need to go back to the heart?
revealSteps.body: Think on your own → tell a partner → be ready to explain. The teacher reveals the answer when the class is ready.

revealSteps.label: THE REASON
revealSteps.title: It needs another push
revealSteps.body: Oxygen is cargo, not a pump. After the lungs the blood has lost most of its push. It returns to the heart so the LEFT ventricle can pump it all the way around the body.
revealSteps.teacherPrompt: Who predicted the push? What did you say?

revealSteps.label: SECOND HEART VISIT
revealSteps.title: Back to the heart: the left side
revealSteps.body: Oxygen-rich blood returns along a vein into the left atrium, then drops through a valve into the left ventricle. Now watch the squeeze.

revealSteps.label: THE HEART SUPPLIES THE FORCE
revealSteps.title: The left ventricle pumps it to the body
revealSteps.body: The left ventricle has the thickest muscle. It contracts and pushes the blood into the main artery (the aorta) and out to the whole body.

revealSteps.label: DELIVERED · REPEAT
revealSteps.title: Oxygen and food reach the body cells
revealSteps.body: In tiny capillaries, oxygen and food move into body cells and waste moves into the blood. The oxygen-poor blood returns to the right atrium, and the journey repeats.
revealSteps.teacherPrompt: Explain the route in one sentence that includes the word “pump”.

question.prompt: Why does oxygen-rich blood go back from the lungs to the heart?

options.text: To pick up more oxygen.
options.feedback: It already picked up oxygen in the lungs. It returns so the heart can pump it to the body.

options.text: Because the lungs pump it back.
options.feedback: The lungs do not pump blood. The lungs add oxygen; the heart does the pumping.

options.text: So the left side of the heart can pump it around the body.
options.feedback: Yes. The blood has oxygen but needs a push. The left side of the heart pumps it all the way around the body.

options.text: To mix with oxygen-poor blood.
options.feedback: Oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor blood do not normally mix. The wall keeps the sides apart.

question.explanation: The lungs supply oxygen. The heart supplies the push. The left side of the heart pumps the oxygen-rich blood around the body.

correct.headline: Correct. Now explain why.
correct.message: The lungs supply oxygen. The heart supplies the push. The left side of the heart pumps the oxygen-rich blood around the body.

incorrect.headline: Let’s fix the idea.

teacherNotes.misconception: A or B: oxygen or the lungs drive the blood.

teacherNotes.ask: Pairs agree each step and must give a reason before you select it. Choose one wrong answer on purpose (e.g. Lungs first) to show the feedback.
teacherNotes.listen: Body → right side → lungs → left side → body, with a reason at each step.
teacherNotes.reason: Each heart side has a different destination; the route repeats.
teacherNotes.misconception: Skipping the second heart visit (lungs → body).
teacherNotes.revisit: Use the sentence frame: “The right side pumps to … ; the left side pumps to …”. Reset and rebuild.

Close with the sentence frame: “The right side pumps to …; the left side pumps to ….”

question.prompt: Which route takes blood from the body and back again?

options.text: Body → lungs → left side of heart → body
options.feedback: This skips the right side, which pumps blood from the body to the lungs.

options.text: Body → right side of heart → lungs → left side of heart → body
options.feedback: Yes. The right side pumps to the lungs; the left side pumps to the body. Both heart visits are needed.

options.text: Body → left side of heart → right side of heart → lungs → body
options.feedback: The lungs must come between the two heart visits.

options.text: Body → right side of heart → body
options.feedback: This skips the lungs, so the blood would never collect oxygen.

question.explanation: Body → right side → lungs → left side → body. Each side of the heart pumps blood to the next place.

correct.headline: Correct. Now explain why.
correct.message: Body → right side → lungs → left side → body. Each side of the heart pumps blood to the next place.

incorrect.headline: Let’s fix the idea.
incorrect.message: Body → right side → lungs → left side → body. Each side of the heart pumps blood to the next place.

teacherNotes.ask: The spotlight student justifies the order; a second pupil checks it.
teacherNotes.listen: Two heart visits with the lungs in between.
teacherNotes.reason: Each heart visit provides a push to a new destination.
teacherNotes.misconception: Option A: skipping the right side.
teacherNotes.revisit: Rebuild the route on screen with the class.
talkingPoints: Ask the spotlight student to say the route aloud while pointing to each place on the diagram.
Two heart visits, with the lungs in between, is the pattern to listen for.

revealSteps.label: NAME BY DIRECTION
revealSteps.title: Away = artery. Towards = vein.
revealSteps.body: Arteries carry blood away from the heart. Veins carry blood back towards the heart. Capillaries are tiny vessels where things are swapped.
revealSteps.teacherPrompt: Choose one vessel. Is it an artery or a vein? How do you know?

revealSteps.label: ZOOM IN · LUNGS
revealSteps.title: In the lungs, oxygen moves into the blood
revealSteps.body: Capillary walls are very thin. Oxygen moves from the air sacs into the blood. Carbon dioxide moves out and is breathed out.
revealSteps.teacherPrompt: What happens to the colour code as the blood collects oxygen?

revealSteps.label: ZOOM IN · BODY
revealSteps.title: At body cells, oxygen and food move out
revealSteps.body: Oxygen and food move from the blood into the body cells. Waste such as carbon dioxide moves from the cells into the blood.
revealSteps.teacherPrompt: Why do body cells need a steady supply of blood?

revealSteps.label: THE ODD ONE OUT
revealSteps.title: A vein full of oxygen-rich blood
revealSteps.body: The vein from the lungs to the heart carries oxygen-rich blood. It is still a vein, because it carries blood TOWARDS the heart.
revealSteps.teacherPrompt: So are vessels named by oxygen or by direction?

teacherNotes.listen: Artery = away, vein = towards; oxygen moves into blood in the lungs and out to cells at the body.
teacherNotes.reason: Thin capillary walls let oxygen, food and waste move between blood and air sacs or cells.
teacherNotes.misconception: All veins carry oxygen-poor blood; blood is really blue.

talkingPoints: Name by direction: arteries go away from the heart, veins come towards it. Trace two vessels together.
Lungs close-up: oxygen moves in, carbon dioxide moves out. Use Slow motion and say it together.
Body close-up: oxygen and food move out to the cells; waste moves into the blood.
Extension (step 4): the vein from the lungs carries oxygen-rich blood. Direction, not oxygen, names a vessel.

question.prompt: What happens as blood passes through the capillaries in the lungs?

options.text: Oxygen moves into the blood and carbon dioxide moves out.
options.feedback: Yes. Oxygen from the air moves into the blood; carbon dioxide moves out to be breathed out.

options.text: The lungs pump the blood to the body.
options.feedback: The lungs do not pump blood. The heart is the pump.

options.text: Oxygen moves out of the blood into the air.
options.feedback: It is the other way round in the lungs: oxygen moves INTO the blood.

options.text: The blood turns blue.
options.feedback: Real blood is always red. Blue is only a diagram code for oxygen-poor blood.

teacherNotes.reason: Exchange happens across thin capillary walls in the lungs.

revealSteps.label: FIND THE MISTAKE
revealSteps.title: A pupil’s route: lungs → foot
revealSteps.body: Discuss with your partner and sketch a corrected route on paper before the teacher shows the repair.
revealSteps.teacherPrompt: What job is missing from this route?

revealSteps.label: REPAIRED
revealSteps.title: Lungs → left side of heart → body
revealSteps.body: The blood had oxygen, but it still needed a push. The left side of the heart pumps it to the foot and the rest of the body.
revealSteps.teacherPrompt: Point to where oxygen is collected. Now point to the pump.

presentation.fallbackNotice: Moving simulations need Schoolynq player 2.9.4-heart4. Older v2.x players show the labelled diagram, the reveal steps and the questions.

teacherNotes.ask: Pupils sketch their repair on paper first. Then select Show the repaired route.
teacherNotes.listen: Add the left side of the heart, with the reason “it pumps the blood to the body”.
teacherNotes.reason: A correct route explains both where oxygen is collected and what pushes the blood onwards.
teacherNotes.misconception: The lungs push blood to the body.
teacherNotes.revisit: Partners point to the oxygen source, then to the pump.
talkingPoints: Pupils sketch their repaired route on paper before you reveal it.
Ask two questions: “Where is oxygen collected?” and “What gives the push?”
Link back to the hinge: collecting oxygen does not replace the pump.

question.prompt: A route sends oxygen-rich blood straight from the lungs to a foot. Which correction explains the missing step?

options.text: Add the lungs again so the blood gets more oxygen.
options.feedback: The blood already has oxygen. It needs the left side of the heart to pump it.

options.text: Add the right side of the heart to mix the blood.
options.feedback: The two sides keep their blood apart. Blood from the lungs goes to the left side.

options.text: Add a vein, because veins pump blood.
options.feedback: Veins carry blood towards the heart. They do not pump. The heart is the pump.

options.text: Add the left side of the heart, because it pumps blood to the foot.
options.feedback: Yes. Lungs → left side of heart → body. The left side supplies the push.

question.explanation: Lungs → left side of heart → body. Collecting oxygen does not replace the need for the heart’s push.

correct.headline: Correct. Now explain why.
correct.message: Lungs → left side of heart → body. Collecting oxygen does not replace the need for the heart’s push.

incorrect.headline: Let’s fix the idea.
incorrect.message: Lungs → left side of heart → body. Collecting oxygen does not replace the need for the heart’s push.

teacherNotes.ask: Ask pupils to compare with their own sketch.
teacherNotes.reason: Oxygen collection and pumping are different jobs.
teacherNotes.misconception: Vessels or lungs do the pumping.
teacherNotes.revisit: Return to the repair screen and replay the repair.
talkingPoints: Ask the spotlight student to compare the correct answer with their own sketch.
Option C (veins pump) shows vessels and the heart being confused. Correct it: vessels carry, the heart pumps.

question.prompt: A red blood cell is in a toe. Which journey comes next?

options.text: vein → right side of heart → lungs → left side of heart → artery
options.feedback: Yes. It returns along a vein to the right side, is pumped to the lungs, returns to the left side and is pumped out along an artery.

options.text: artery → lungs → body
options.feedback: Blood leaving a toe travels towards the heart in a vein, and it must visit the heart before the lungs.

options.text: vein → left side of heart → lungs → right side of heart
options.feedback: Blood from the body reaches the RIGHT side first.

options.text: vein → lungs → right side of heart → body
options.feedback: The right side must pump the blood to the lungs first.

question.explanation: Toe → vein → right side → lungs → left side → artery → body. Two heart visits, each giving a push.

correct.headline: Correct. Now explain why.
correct.message: Toe → vein → right side → lungs → left side → artery → body. Two heart visits, each giving a push.

incorrect.headline: Let’s fix the idea.
incorrect.message: Toe → vein → right side → lungs → left side → artery → body. Two heart visits, each giving a push.

teacherNotes.ask: Use as the whole-class close after paper slips are collected.
teacherNotes.listen: A, with both heart visits named.
teacherNotes.reason: Route plus vessel direction plus pumping.

glossary.heart: a muscular organ that pumps blood around the body.
glossary.atrium: an upper chamber of the heart (plural: atria). It collects blood coming back to the heart.
glossary.ventricle: a lower chamber of the heart. Its thick muscle pumps blood out of the heart.
glossary.septum: the wall of muscle between the right and left sides of the heart. It stops the two kinds of blood mixing.
glossary.valve: a flap that lets blood flow only one way.
glossary.artery: a blood vessel that carries blood away from the heart.
glossary.vein: a blood vessel that carries blood towards the heart.
glossary.capillary: a tiny blood vessel with very thin walls, where oxygen, food and waste move in and out.
glossary.circulation: the movement of blood around the body, pumped by the heart through blood vessels.
glossary.plasma: the liquid part of blood. It carries dissolved food and waste.
glossary.red blood cell: a blood cell that carries most of the oxygen.
glossary.oxygen: a gas from the air that body cells need. It enters the blood in the lungs.
glossary.carbon dioxide: a waste gas made by body cells. The blood carries it to the lungs to be breathed out.
glossary.contract: to squeeze or get shorter. When heart muscle contracts, it pushes blood out.
glossary.pulse: the beat you can feel in an artery each time the heart pumps.
glossary.blood: a red liquid that carries oxygen, food and waste around the body.
glossary.muscle: body tissue that can contract (squeeze) to make something move. The heart is made of muscle.
glossary.pump: something that pushes a liquid along. The heart pumps blood.
glossary.lungs: the organs where oxygen from the air enters the blood and carbon dioxide leaves it.
glossary.right side: the person’s right side of the heart (shown on your left in a front view). It pumps blood to the lungs.
glossary.left side: the person’s left side of the heart (shown on your right in a front view). It pumps blood to the body.

faq.q: Why is the vessel from the lungs to the heart a vein if it carries oxygen-rich blood?
faq.a: Vessels are named by direction, not by oxygen. A vein carries blood towards the heart. The pulmonary vein brings oxygen-rich blood from the lungs back to the heart, so it is a vein. The pulmonary artery is the opposite case: an artery carrying oxygen-poor blood away from the heart to the lungs.

faq.q: Why is the left ventricle wall thicker than the right?
faq.a: The left ventricle pumps blood all around the body, a much longer route, so it needs more force. The right ventricle only pumps blood to the lungs, which are close by. More work means more muscle, so the left wall is thicker.

faq.q: Do the two sides of the heart take turns?
faq.a: No. In each heartbeat both atria squeeze together, then both ventricles squeeze together. The model follows one cell slowly, which can make it look like turns. Say this explicitly when you show the journey.

faq.q: What makes the lub-dub sound of the heart?
faq.a: The sounds are made by valves closing. “Lub” is the valves between the atria and ventricles closing as the ventricles start to squeeze. “Dub” is the valves at the start of the arteries closing as the ventricles relax.

faq.q: How fast does a child's heart beat?
faq.a: At rest, most children of this age have a heart rate of roughly 70 to 100 beats per minute, and it rises with exercise. The Workbook’s pulse investigation (Unit 1.1 Challenge) uses 72 beats per minute sitting still. The model is slowed down on purpose and is not a real heart rate.

faq.q: What is the difference between a pulse and a heartbeat?
faq.a: A heartbeat is the heart squeezing. A pulse is the stretch you feel in an artery, for example at the wrist or neck, each time the heart pushes blood into it. So the pulse rate matches the heart rate.

faq.q: Why does blood need to go to the lungs at all?
faq.a: To collect oxygen from the air we breathe in and to get rid of carbon dioxide, which we breathe out. Body cells need a steady supply of oxygen, so blood keeps returning to the lungs.

faq.q: Why does blood go slowly through capillaries?
faq.a: There are huge numbers of capillaries, so the blood is shared out between them and moves slowly in each one. Slow flow gives time for oxygen, food and waste to pass through the very thin capillary walls.

faq.q: Does the heart get its own blood supply?
faq.a: Yes. The heart is a muscle, so it needs oxygen too. Small arteries on its surface, the coronary arteries, carry oxygen-rich blood to the heart muscle itself. This is extension content.
Valves are flaps that let blood flow only one way: from each atrium down into its ventricle, and from each ventricle out into its artery. They stop blood flowing backwards when the heart squeezes.

faq.q: Why do we say oxygen-poor and not 'without oxygen'?
faq.a: Blood returning from the body still carries some oxygen; it has just given a lot of it to body cells. The Workbook says “without oxygen” as a simplification. “Oxygen-poor” is more accurate and still easy for Stage 6.

faq.q: What if a pupil mentions a hole in the heart?
faq.a: Some babies are born with a gap in the wall between the two sides. Doctors can often close it. Answer briefly and kindly, without details about any pupil or family member, and offer to talk after the lesson.
